On Clause 1-Section 118-General Averaging

Section 118 has to do
with averaging and it is a new provision. With regard to this principle of averaging, we must recognize that the present Income Tax Act contains a number of averaging provisions which would tend to smooth out the progressive rate structure of a taxpayer who has an unusually high income in the year because he has received certain specified types of income during that year. For instance, if he has been repaid a lump sum out of a pension plan, if he has exercised his rights under an employee stock option plan, or if he has had a property on which he has claimed depreciation, has sold it and there is a recapture of the capital cost allowance, he may then average out. However, there are limitations as to that.
In any event, Bill C-259 will eventually eliminate all the present averaging provisions except those applicable to farmers and fishermen, and it will replace them with two averaging provisions available to all individuals. First, there will be a general averaging provision which applies regardless of the type of income, and second, an income averaging annuity provisions which applies only where special types of income have been received. The use of the latter does not affect the first type. In other words, the utilization of the second form of averaging will not affect the first form because the latter will be instituted directly and automatically by the Department of National Revenue.
The general averaging proposal we are considering in section 118 follows that contained in the white paper. It will apply in any year in which the individual's income is (a) at least 110 per cent of the immediately preceding year, and (b), 120 per cent of the average income for the four immediately preceding years. Let us illustrate this by an example.
Let us assume that in the four preceding years the income was $30,000 but in the fifth year, for some particular reason, the income goes to $36,000. Now, let us apply the tests to see whether that $6,000 could be averaged in any way to smooth out the rather dramatic escalation that there will be in tax due to the progressive tax system. Under the first test, that is, at least 110 per cent of the immediately preceding year's income, 110 per cent would be $33,000. So therefore since the income is $36,000 it has passed test (a). Now, let us look at test (b), which says that the income has to be at least 120 per cent of the average income for the four immediately preceding years. If you take 120 per cent of $30,000 it comes to $36,000, and so, unfortunately, the income does not exceed the 120 per cent of the average of the four immediately preceding years. There is no averaging excess, and therefore there is
[The Assistant Deputy Chairman.)
no way that the general averaging will be available. So, one has to be very careful about this.
I suppose that to consider this we could go into certain refinements. But in the year of death of a taxpayer, for instance, the averaging formula will be read as if the percentages in what I call (a) and (b)-the (a) being 110 per cent of the preceding year, and the (b) being 120 per cent of the four preceding years-as though those percentages were 100 per cent, and this concession is not available if the executors elect to file a separate return in respect of rights or things receivable at death. This is another very complicated provision of income tax for consultants and auditors. But let us have a look at the transition. This does not come into effect in 1972. The general averaging provision I referred to is not available for 1972, and in the years 1973, 1974 and 1975 the formula will be applied as if condition (b), that is, the 120 per cent of the four immediately preceding years, were to read respectively one, two and three years, so that by 1976 it will be into the full four years.
The existing averaging provisions deal with employee stock options, the sale of inventory and receivables, authors, and combined income and capital receipts, and may be used by individuals for tax years ending in 1972 and 1973. These are matters of detail. The present averaging rules covering recaptured capital cost allowance and incorrect inventory valuation will continue for individuals for the taxation years ending before 1976. Neither the new general averaging provision nor the transitional provisions are available to corporations which, under the present act, can average on certain of these items, such as recaptured capital cost allowance.
It is said that these rules are somewhat more generous than those proposed in the white paper, and to that extent I suppose they are an improvement. Mr. Chairman, it was very easy to improve on the white paper. May I say that I do not know who was responsible for all of these changes. I do not think the finance committee should take any credit here because, frankly, the moves in here are so elaborate and complicated that they go beyond the ken of the average member of this House to thread his way through them, and we would need the advice of tax consultants. So, while we recognize that some of the new sections are going to provide some benefits, all taxpayers should know that there are limits to them. Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I am quite prepared to accept the changes made, to the extent that they are an improvement over the white paper. They are not as generous as individuals might have wanted, but I think they are better than what had originally been offered.
In his statement today to the provincial finance ministers, the Minister of Finance indicated that undoubtedly there would have to be many amendments next year and in the following year to provide for inequities that might show up, and that in any event, if there were inequities that could not be corrected by changes in the Income Tax Act in the immediate future there would always be a form of relief that could be granted under the Financial Administration Act. From past experience, Mr. Chairman, I can say that holding out this hope of relief under the Financial Administration Act is almost like telling an individual he may be forgiven his sins providing he can climb up and see the Lord Almighty to get forgiveness.

Teachers' Federation had a supplementary pension plan whereby funds were paid into a national trust company under the trust plan and were then transferred to a credit union run by the B.C. teachers under the security of a note. These funds were then used by the borrowers, the teachers, to build homes in central and rural areas of British Columbia.
Some 1,250 teachers participate in this registered retirement savings plan in British Columbia, and there are 72 in Alberta as of July 1, 1971. The amount invested in the fund at that time was $1,650,000. The plan is designed to enable members of the plan to designate at the time of subscribing to the plan and at annual intervals thereafter the amount to be contributed to each of the investment income sections and the equity section. Funds contributed to the investment income sections are paid over to the trustee who is free to invest in notes of the B.C. federation and co-operative association so long as the association is prepared to receive them at current rates.
Under the new section that describes what is a qualified investment the notes signed by the teachers' federation co-operative are not qualified. They will not be covered by this section unless some change in the bill is made by the

government so as to include this type of investment under the heading of "qualified investment". The government can either make a specific amendment to this effect or utilize the provision contained in section 146(l)(g)(iv) which provides:
-such other investments as may be prescribed by regulations of the Governor in Council made on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance-
The plan to which I have referred provides a supplementary pension for the teachers, most of whom are within ten or 15 years of retirement and want to supplement their pensions with a savings plan. They started teaching at a time when teachers' salaries 'were very low and therefore the contributions to and interest in their pension plans are rather slim.
I think the teachers have done a very fine job, not only on their own behalf but also in providing credit funds for building homes and other facilities for teachers in outlying areas where no other credit facility will venture. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not go to these areas, the banks will not go and the conventional insurance companies will not go. It seems to me it would be a tragedy if some rather too rigidly drawn provision- which, by the way, is an amendment to the Income Tax Act-should knock this completely on the head.
I have been talking to the solicitors representing the teachers' federation and co-operative, and they have not been able to devise any other way whereby the form of security is one that would qualify under the presently enumerated paragraphs of section 146(l)(g). Therefore I make this plea to the parliamentary secretary, and through him to the minister, that since the teachers' federation have presented their case to the government, the government should be able to decide now whether this will be allowed to go forward.
I also want to make reference to section 146(2) which deals with the acceptance by the minister of registered retirement savings plans. It seems to me that in the past an almost scandalous situation has existed whereby the Minister of National Revenue and his officials have held plans in abeyance for a long time. I want to know whether this situation has now been cleared up and, if so, under what conditions. Or am I confusing this with some other type of plan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Pension plans.

Then that is fine; I shall withdraw my comments in that regard. But what I am concerned about is this: In the case of non-acceptance by the minister, what recourse does an individual have? Does he have any appeal if certain steps are taken? Surely it would not be to the Tax Review Board-but would an appeal lie to the Federal Court? Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would consult his officials, who have much more detailed knowledge of this legislation, and tell us what is the situation. After all, subsection (2) provides:
The minister shall not accept for registration for the purposes of this act any retirement savings plan unless, in his opinion-
This is great, because it is tied to the opinion of the minister and his ability to exercise discretion as to adherence and compliance with certain requirements laid out in
November 2, 1971

the section. I should like to know what recourse an individual or a group of individuals might have who want to qualify a bona fide registered retirement savings plan which the minister or his officials have deemed not to comply with the subsection. To some extent the same thing would apply to subsection (3) where we find the words, "The minister may accept", and so on.
Let me turn to subsection (5) and again ask for an explanation from the parliamentary secretary. While there is a modification here, I should like him to confirm that the date February 28 is still the operative date in respect of any registered retirement savings plan. If an individual wishes to exercise his option during the first two months of 1972, can he qualify for a registered retirement savings plan for 1971 and be entitled to deduct the appropriate contributions made in 1971 from his net income before arriving at his taxable income?
Then I should like an explanation of subsection (6). What can be done for the disposition of non-qualified investments? May I say here that I have run into problems where a taxpayer has changed his or her mind regarding a registered retirement savings plan. The contribution was put forward but the deduction was not made on the income tax return. As a result of misunderstandings we do encounter situations where an individual may be chastised, or it may be put to the taxpayer that he furnished improper information in the return. I suppose every case depends on the circumstances. In any event, I should like a full explanation of subsection (6).
We then have a whole series of new subsections-(9), (10) and (11). I should like an explanation from the parliamentary secretary in respect of these. This section has 16 subsections, but many of the others are carried forward from the present act and I need not go into them in detail or get explanations in that regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to reply briefly to the remarks of the hon. member who has just spoken in respect of the position of the B.C. teachers regarding section 146(l)(g). As the hon. member has suggested, the B.C. Teachers' Federation sent representatives to Ottawa to meet with all persons concerned, including the B.C. caucus, to discuss problems which have arisen pertaining to the provisions of section 146.
As I understand it, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance will be commenting on this matter shortly. But as I understand it, the government is extremely sympathetic to the views of the B.C. teachers who have a particular form of investment which, as it now stands, offends the provisions of the bill before this House. Theoretically, we should move to amend the act in order to correct this deficiency. However, the B.C. caucus in unanimity has taken up the problem with the Minister of Finance, his parliamentary secretary and officials of the department and we are assured that by virtue of the provisions of section 146 regulations will be passed to accommodate the peculiar position of the B.C. teachers pertaining to their investment in their retirement savings plan.
We ask, as the hon. member for Edmonton West has asked, why it is that we do not move to amend the act? The government's position and the position of the B.C. caucus is precisely that any move to amend the statute at
Income Tax Act
this stage would pro.bably accommodate many other situations which offend the substance of the provisions we are considering in section 146 and would permit further tax avoidances which section 146 as it now stands is designed to prevent.
There is no doubt in the minds of the B.C. caucus that the government will be moving more or less with the passage of this act to provide by regulation-
What is the B.C. caucus?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: What group is this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As far as we are concerned, the B.C. caucus is made up of government members on this side of the House. The government will be moving by regulation to accommodate this organization and such other organizations in the country that can show themselves to be bona fide and within the purview and substance of this particular provision of the bill.

It is very touching to note that there is a sub-party or sub-group in this House which seems to have taken up the cudgel. It is quite proper that B.C. members should do that. I, too, met with the B.C. teachers. It came to my attention, through another source, that they were down here to see me. I did speak about this on a previous occasion, and that possibly inspired the hon. member to make some inquiries.
I must say the suggestion that the government will pass regulations governing this and other bodies, if they can show they are affected in the same way, is one thing. But this does not deal with the problem of individual members of the teachers' federation who want to know whether they should continue making payments into the retirement savings plan. They want to know now, not six months hence. They are not interested in the suggestion that in the normal course of events-and that is very slow when it comes to the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue-regulations will be passed permitting these people to go forward.
Since their plan was registered, legal and in existence, nothing should be done now by bringing in an amendment to the act which would nullify the present plan and its arrangements. It is perfectly bona fide, and surely to goodness the 1,200 or more members in this savings plan are entitled to an answer now. I trust the parliamentary secretary will give an answer, or at least an undertaking to answer. I do not want to indicate the name of a particular official because he is not in a position to answer in this House, but he is here and has had a good deal to do with this. At the committee hearings he would be questioned by me and other members.
This question goes back many months. I am sure there is good will all the way but I am concerned about the time element and what the people who participate in this plan are to be told. What are they to do? Are they to suspend their payments? After all, they have an obligation under their contract with the trust company. Would they place themselves in default, and would their contract be in
24372-27i

Income Tax Act
default if they did not make the payment? This is a question which must be answered.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words with respect to this section. I believe the hon. member for Edmonton West has missed the main point made by the hon. member for New Westminster. While we are all in sympathy with the predicament in which the B.C. Teachers' Federation retirement savings plan is involved, we have all been well briefed and have thoroughly discussed this matter on behalf of the teachers' federation. We must also realize that by virtue of the fact that it is a change or a departure from a previous list of the type of investment which can be accepted by the Minister of Finance, there are also such organizations as the B.C. central retirement savings plan and there will be others.
With regard to the time element, I think we all understand that the proclamation of the bill will not be made on the day the bill is passed. This will give the Minister of Finance plenty of time in which to hear submissions from various other organizations. I am quite confident that the B.C. Teachers' Federation would be sympathetic to similar types of organizations in other parts of Canada which may have within their organizations the criteria to obtain agreement from the Minister of Finance that a change should be made and that they should be included as well. I think this is the vital and important feature to be considered.
Amendment of the bill on behalf of the B.C. Teachers' Federation retirement savings plan would be acceptable, I presume, so far as we are concerned. It certainly would be so far as I am concerned and so far as my colleagues are concerned. We feel, however, that the more appropriate way would be to provide them with the necessary legislation through regulations subsequent to the passage of this bill. Therefore, I would support my colleague from New Westminster and I should like to assure the B.C. Teachers' Federation that we certainly feel, after exhaustive examination and discussion, that this is a better method by which to bring about a solution to the problem and to provide them with the necessary machinery so that they will be able to carry on without any problems in the interim. I would therefore hope we can continue on that basis on behalf of the federation.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief because the hon. member for Edmonton West, the hon. member for Fraser Valley East and I all heard the same representations from what one might call, in all kindness, a very good lobby group and we might all say much the same thing. The question of the slowness and the uncertainty which has been raised is something which hits just about every other group affected by this section.
Candidly, I cannot see that it is a serious objection. I should like to point out that the particular plan we are talking about is one which is financed out of the pockets of the teachers who contribute. It is not the situation of a company or its employees contributing to a fund which they in turn-although they call it a retirement fund-use for the purpose of the business of the company. This is not a device to do something outside their control; it is a legitimate way of protecting themselves for the future, after retirement. I am sure many members know that

until very recently the provisions for the retirement of teachers in British Columbia and Alberta had been very poor.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley East raised the point that the British Columbia central retirement savings plan, which is substantially the same as the B.C. Central Credit Union, has exceptions in respect of the regulations for the British Columbia teachers. Will those exceptions apply in a generic sense to other organizations just the same as to the British Columbia central retirement savings plan and other such schemes?
I quite agree that the government is correct in its attempt to plug the hole in the income tax regulation whereby it is possible to put money into a retirement savings plan, lend it back and have it used by the company and thus be a device by which to get around the tax law. In at least these two instances, however, I feel the people have acted in good faith in setting up such a scheme.
I should like to know exactly what the proposals are in respect of the regulations and whether not only these two but similar organizations might be involved. While we have talked consistently about the B.C. teachers' retirement pension plan, there is a similar plan in operation in the province of Alberta. This is not strictly a matter of personal interest to British Columbia, in my opinion: we are dealing with an issue which is general to the country at large. I promised to speak briefly, Mr. Chairman, and I trust I have done so.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a word of dissatisfaction on my own part with the way in which the government proposes to deal with deferred profitsharing plans which are in effect, which have been in existence and under which in many cases very considerable contributions have been made. Under the present law a deferred profit-sharing plan is an extremely attractive way in which to save for retirement. The employee of a company makes contributions and at retirement, under the present law, he has been able to draw out the substantial sum that has been built up during his working career and invest it in a small business. In the case, for example, of the Simpsons-Sears deferred profit-sharing plan, this is frequently done.
The proposals in the bill before us permit continued favoured treatment to the pay-out provided that the retiree invests his savings in a pension. If he continues to do what has been traditional in the past, that is, if he takes the money out and invests it in a business or in other capital assets, it is taxed at an extremely heavy rate compared to the previous treatment it enjoyed. I would ask the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance to give consideration to the possibility of permitting this continued favourable treatment for investments in preferred profit-sharing plans, especially when the assets are withdrawn and used for investment in the capital assets of a business.
It is one thing for someone who has saved all his working life in a deferred profit-sharing plan and who retires, draws the money out and spends it on improving his home or in some other form of consumption, say in retirement
November 2, 1971

travelling or making gifts or something of that nature, but it is another where a person continues to invest the money but rather than investing it in an annuity he invests it in a small business or in a capital asset. For these people there are ways of providing a more equitable tax treatment.
The parliamentary secretary will recall the days when the finance committee operated and a number of methods of achieving this result were put forward. I proposed one myself and I am disappointed that it was not possible for the minister, in the bill which he proposed, to consider this important situation. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will not inform me that all hope should be abandoned, because if that is the case it will be a grave setback to the deferred profit-sharing plans of many corporations which have been of great benefit to the country.
I have a question for the parliamentary secretary. Has he received many representations regarding the particular item mentioned by the hon. member for Don Valley?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should say that the only representation I have received on this particular item has been from the Simpsons-Sears deferred profit-sharing plan. However, that is a personal answer and does not necessarily reflect the representations that may have been received either by the minister or by the Department of Finance. I am afraid I do not have an assessment of what the volume of representations may have been in that respect.

The question which I intended to ask was whether there were many companies that had this type of plan. Logically, if a great many companies had this type of plan, maybe they should receive general consideration. I wonder if the government has looked at this question to see whether they might give more equitable treatment to these employees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Of course, the problem here is not only one of more equitable treatment, but perhaps I will deal with that when I have an opportunity to respond to the various general representations that have been made. There are a number of companies, probably a couple of dozen-I am reminded of Dofasco, the Dominion Foundry and Steel Company-that have this type of set up, as well as Simpsons-Sears and one or two of the oil companies in my own area; and there are a few others.
It is not a plan that is widely used in terms of the business community, but where it is used it is certainly one to which the people who have implemented it seem to have a very deep attachment. The problem that arises here and to which they are really objecting is the substitution of the current very favourable averaging provisions under section 36 of the present act on some payments taken out of the deferred sharing plan. Section 36 will continue in effect under the new tax regime for contributions made up to the end of the current year, but for contributions made in 1972 and beyond, the general averaging provisions which the committee approved earlier today will apply and the favourable averaging provisions under section 36 will be replaced by those provisions.

Mr. Chairman, I rise for the purpose of asking the parliamentary secretary whether he will comment on the matters which have been raised with respect
Income Tax Act
to the B.C. teachers' retirement plan. I do not think there is any necessity to repeat what has already been put before the parliamentary secretary. We would like to know what amendments he would be prepared to move or to accept, particularly with reference to the one point at issue in section 146(g), or whether there is some way under the regulations by which he proposes to deal with the situation which has been described-because there is no doubt that in section 146(g) the government is trying to prevent some of the abuses that have taken place.
There is always the possibility of a retirement plan being used to benefit the members in some way other than just for retirement purposes. But I think it is fairly clear from all the data which I have seen and from discussions with those who are interested in this plan that the B.C. teachers' retirement plan has not been used to benefit the members directly but has become a co-operative that has made it possible for teachers all over B.C. to borrow money to build houses. The advantage has been that the interest rates are fair and reasonable.
More important, the interest rates are uniform across the province, with the result that a teacher in Tofino can borrow money at the same rate as a teacher in Vancouver or Burnaby. This has been very helpful in providing housing accommodation for teachers all over the province of British Columbia. I do not need to labour the point; I am sure the minister is familiar with it. I understand that the representatives of the B.C. teachers' retirement plan discussed the matter with the parliamentary secretary and received a very sympathetic hearing. My reason for rising was to ask the parliamentary secretary whether he has reached any conclusion regarding how this problem might be resolved.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I certainly did not intend to avoid responding to this question. However, it seemed to me that there was a certain amount of home cooking going on around the chamber and I wanted to give all hon. members who wished to get their cases on the record an opportunity to have their say before I answered. However, if no other hon. members wish to discuss this point I shall be delighted to deal with it now.
The B.C. central retirement savings plan, which is the creature of the B.C. Central Credit Union, and the B.C. Teachers' Federation retirement savings plan, which operates through the B.C. Teachers' Federation Co-operative Association, both made very persuasive arguments to the government in respect of the problem with which they are confronted-the intervention at this point of the sections defining qualified investments. There is no question that the method by which these organizations have invested up to this point their extra pension funds-and of course this is over and above the statutory pensions with which B.C. teachers are provided in the ordinary course of events by the school boards, and so on-is not at present, under the bill before us, an authorized investment. The hon. member for Edmonton West described that rather fully so I will not reiterate what he said.
Hon. members have noted that the reason for defining qualified investments is to prevent the eventuality of a taxpayer who has deferred taxation as a result of the provisions of the tax bill that permit retirement savings to be accumulated tax free and tax deferred until the bene-

November 2, 1971
Income Tax Act
fits are drawn out to somehow or other filter back and become available for the personal use of the taxpayer or of people who are not at arms length with him. So there are some general rules provided in the bill that will govern that situation.
There is provision in section 146(l)(g)(iv) for the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, to prescribe by regulation additional types of investments to those specifically enumerated or referred to in the section. It is the intention of the Minister of Finance to recommend to the Governor in Council that regulations be adopted which will effectively solve the problem of the two bodies with which we are concerned.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am not in a position at this point to give the details of those, but I am sure the criteria will involve the number of members of the credit union and perhaps even the longevity of such a credit union before it starts to offer its securities for this purpose. However, I can give the assurance to hon. members-there have been representations from all sides of the House and in particular, I am reminded, from the B.C. caucus, whoever they may be-that I am sure when the recommendations are made public the organizations concerned will be satisfied. I am also conscious of the problem that the hon. member for Edmonton West emphasized, of the necessity of these organizations to know now that their investment policies will not be proscribed in the future. I am pleased to have the opportunity to give that assurance, and I hope they will now be able to proceed with an easier mind.
Hon. members have raised other matters in the course of the debate. I think that in responding to the specific questions of the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley I perhaps answered the hon. member for Don Valley as well, in dealing with the rather specific problems that were raised by the Simpsons-Sears deferred profit-sharing plan management, among others. I am sorry the answer is not more favourable, but the proponents of that plan and of other profit-sharing plans have presented their case very eloquently to the Minister of Finance and to the department.
I can assure the House that there is no retroactive penalty or effect in the provisions of the bill with respect to those plans, but for future contributions beyond the end of the current year the general averaging provisions, rather than the very favourable averaging provisions which pertain under section 36 of the present act, will apply. The general averaging provisions are not in fact as advantageous to the taxpayers as those special provisions are in the case of lump sum withdrawals from deferred profit-sharing plans.
The hon. member for Edmonton West has raised a number of specific questions involving subsections (5), (6), (9), (10) and (11).
And subsection (2).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
And subsection (2). I am getting a little confused, as we call "bingo" here, with the subsections of section 146. I will deal with these seriatim as well. So far
as subsection (2) is concerned, this is the same as the present subsection 79B(b). This subsection, together with subsection (3), describes the requirements to be met by a plan if it is to be accepted for registration by the Minister of National Revenue. The plan must provide that the proceeds be taken as an annuity for life. The whole purpose of retirement savings plans is to provide for those who cannot become members of a pension plan, or people who have an inadequate pension plan, to defer tax on amounts set aside for retirement income. For this reason the rules concerning these plans, and in particular the rules about the use of proceeds, are designed to be comparable to the rules under which pension plans operate. With respect to subsection (5)-

Mr. Chairman, the particular point I raised was not so much questioning the regulations or requirements of the plan but what provision is there if there is an honest difference of opinion? Is it the minister's decision that is final, and where do we now turn, if at all, for any particular type of appeal? Here I am relying on the encyclopedic knowledge of the officials.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I would refer the hon. member to section 172(3). If when he has perused that he has further questions, I will be pleased to answer them or try to answer them. Dealing with subsection (5) this, again, is the same as the present provisions of the bill in subsection 79B(5), except that the limits on the amount of a premium that may be deducted from income have been increased. The new limits are, first, where the individual is a member of a registered pension plan to which contributions are made by an employer, an amount that when added to the amount deducted by him for the year of the pension plan contribution does not exceed the lesser of $2,500 or 20 per cent of his earned income, and where the individual is not a member of a registered pension plan, the limit is the lesser of $4,000 or 20 per cent of his earned income. The present limits of $1,500 and $2,500 are replaced by the limits of $2,500 and $4,000 to which I have referred. No change has been made with regard to the limit of 20 per cent of earned income.
With respect to subsection (6), Mr. Chairman, this is part of the new rules for the investment of trust and other savings plans. It provides relief for the penalty imposed for non-qualified investment. This should be read in conjunction with subsection (10) which requires that the cost of a non-qualified investment made by a trust should be included in the income of the annuitant. Where a trust disposes of a non-qualified investment an amount equal to that amount included in the purchase cost may be deducted from the annuitant's income. If a non-qualified investment is disposed of for less than cost, then only the proceeds of disposition may be deducted.
With respect to subsection (9), again this is part of the new rules. It requires that the amounts shall be included in the income of the annuitant under the plan where a trust sells trust property for less than its value or buys property at greater than its value. I think I dealt with this matter at greater length in response to a question by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants. One would not ordinarily expect such an eventuality to arise except in transactions that were not at arms length, and this to

November 2, 1971

avoid a tax deferred income to people with whom the annuitant is dealing on a non-arms length basis.
Subsection (10) imposes a penalty where a trust governed by a registered retirement savings plan acquires a non-qualified investment or uses trust property as security for a loan. The penalty is an amount equal to the cost of the non-qualified investment or the value of the property used as security, and requires that it be included in the income of the annuitant under the plan. And, as I mentioned earlier, that should be read in conjunction with subsection (6).
Subsection (11), again, is part of the new rules concerning investments of a trust for retirement savings plans. The definition of qualified investment for retirement savings plans does not include life insurance contracts, but this will permit a trust to hold certain kinds of insurance contracts. The policies described are the same as those which may be held by a trust for a deferred profit-sharing plan as described in section 198(6) of the bill. The cash surrender value must not be less than the amount insured at a certain time before the seventy-first birthday of the insured person.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that I have responded to the specific questions which have been asked. If I have missed any, I welcome reminders from hon. members opposite.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the parliamentary secretary a question? I know that those who are interested in the B.C. teachers' retirement plan will be most appreciative of the statement just made by the parliamentary secretary. There is no doubt that this question can be dealt with much more expeditiously by regulation than by a complicated amendment here. Is the parliamentary secretary in a position to make any commitment that such a change in the regulations will be made almost immediately after the act is proclaimed, in order that there may not be any gap in time during which the matter of investments could be called in question?
If there is any hiatus in that regard, serious legal complications could result. If the parliamentary secretary could give me an assurance in this regard it would ease the minds of those who are concerned about this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, without being able to say when the provision will be promulgated by the Governor in Council, I can assure the hon. member that its terms will be such that no gap will exist.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to ask the parliamentary secretary whether he thinks that the legislation respecting profit-sharing plans will have the effect of phasing out this type of arrangement between employer and employee. I ask this question because I feel that this type of arrangement with the employees of certain companies has gone a long way toward maintaining excellent employer-employee relations and has worked to the benefit of both employer and employee. I wonder if the people who have such profitsharing plans are satisfied with the legislation. In fact, I know they are not completely satisfied. Does the parliamentary secretary think that those people can live with
Income Tax Act
the legislation, or will it have, as might be suggested, the effect of phasing out such arrangements?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it should not have that effect and I do not think it will have that effect. I believe the effect will be this: it will treat this type of plan, which is a method of providing for retirement savings, in exactly the same way as it treats other methods of providing for the same eventuality. Both registered retirement savings plans and pension plans will be so treated. Lump sum payments with respect to those plans will be treated in a similar fashion rather than being given the extremely favourable treatment under section 36 of the present act.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary referred me to section 172(3). Most of us are not familiar with this part of the bill because these are entirely new sections. I notice that that section comes in a total block dealing with the Tax Review Board and the Federal Court of Appeal, and therefore any commentary on these matters ought to be made when that section is considered. This is a very convenient block which I hope we will get to before too long.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask a short question that arises out of a phrase on page 390, subsection (2)(a)(i), which provides:
(a) the plan does not
(i) provide for the payment of any benefit before maturity, except by way of a refund of premiums-
My question arises out of that phrase and may interest the B.C. teachers, among others. Since this is rapidly becoming a country of nomads in which people cross provincial boundaries, my question is pertinent. A person may work for a short while as a teacher in British Columbia, Nova Scotia or what-have-you and then move. All that person can look for, I take it, will be a return of premiums paid with respect to this plan. I take it that the language of this subsection means that he cannot get interest on the money that is being applied to these savings plans and that after letters are exchanged back and forth that person may get his money returned without any other benefit or interest. In other words, he merely gets a straight cash return. Am I correct in assuming that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the word "premium" and the phrase "refund of premiums" have rather unusual meanings in this section. I would refer the hon. member to the definition section contained in subsection 146(l)(f) in the case of "premium" and to subsection 146(l)(h) in the case of the definition "refund of premiums". Essentially, however, the hon. member is correct. The plan, to qualify, must provide that the proceeds will be taken as an annuity for life, and the only thing that the member may get back is his contribution.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question? Shall section 146 as amended carry?

Agreed.
Clause 1, section 146, as amended, agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, there are two new provisions here and I should like to deal with one of them. I did ask a question earlier of the parliamentary secretary which arose in part from the new provisions on page 48, but obviously capital gains are not dealt with here. The section I intend to raise is subsection (5) which deals with a shareholder who has the benefit of an automobile. I suppose in some ways this is the counterpart of an employee who has the benefit of an automobile.
I take it this provision really deals with the income of people in Canada. If a corporation which is not even resident in Canada or does not carry on business primarily in Canada provides the use of an automobile for a shareholder and he does not meet the entire cost of the automobile-this is a simplification of the situation-it must be counted as income. Am I correct in interpreting this provision in that way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This is very comparable to the provision we discussed under section 6(l)(e) when we were dealing
Income Tax Act
with an employee who had the use of an automobile provided by his employer. This deals with the situation where a company provides an automobile to a shareholder and makes that a taxable benefit.

If you look at section 6(l)(e) and section 15(5) you will see that they are the stand-by charges for automobiles. The wording is the same and they are subject to the same disabilities or difficulties. Why should there be a difference if the automobile is leased or owned by the employer? Why should there be a different formula? If the car is owned or leased by the company, why should this make any difference to the shareholder? This suggests that section 6(2) is applicable mutatis mutandis with section 5, so we are dealing with precisely the same sort of thing. Why is this not on the basis or theory that there is an aliquot portion per month or value of the automobile? Why is it not on that basis?
The hon. member for Calgary Centre asked what sort of solution is to be provided for the difficulties of an automobile salesman. A salesman on straight commission might be using a demonstrator car for his personal use. It may be a very valuable car. Two weeks later he may be using a standard model which has a much lower value. This could easily be true of a salesman who works for a multi-model agency. I will not name one because I might offend hon. members who have a liking for a different automobile manufacturer. But if you walk down a few blocks from this edifice you might find a Chevrolet, Oldsmobile, Cadillac agency. A salesman there might be furnished with a Chevrolet car for a period of a month, then he might be given an Oldsmobile and, subsequently, a Cadillac. There is quite a difference in the selling price of those vehicles. How do you work out this formula in that situation?
If the taxpayer happens to be a shareholder in the company owning the dealership, the same questions would have to be asked. Why should there be these differences? Why is this not simply worked on the basis of a proportionate value of the automobile, because in cases where different automobiles are made available you run into trouble. This question of leasing or owning a car involves the use of a different formula, particularly under section 6, and that is a lot of nonsense.

That is part of the weekly
swindle-sheet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think it is the practice of the Department of National Revenue, where an individual is both an employee and a shareholder, to look at him as an employee for this purpose. We did not run into that kind of confusion, or at least that was my experience when I was in both positions and had a company car. Those were the good old days.
All I can say is that the parliamentary secretary's confusion must be compounded, because section 6 is worse than that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The question raised the other day by the hon. member for Calgary Centre regarding salesmen for automobile companies is one we have undertaken to look at. There is a problem which is recognized, and certainly
24372-28)

November 2, 1971
Income Tax Act
any rectification of that problem will be effective for the whole of the 1972 taxation year.

Why is there a different formula in respect of leasing compared with owning an automobile? Section 6 ties into section 15 by cross-reference, so my remarks regarding the complications of section 6 are fully germane. Why is there a distinction between leasing and owning a vehicle? It provides for different formulas for charging a taxpayer who operates a vehicle under lease or one that is owned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The value of the unit is what is assessed for the purpose of the taxpayer. There is obviously a different cost to the employer depending on whether he leases or owns the car provided the employee or the shareholder, and hence the value is different.

With the greatest respect, I find that this is similar to determining the value of a horse by its rear end. It is the benefit to the taxpayer or the employee that is important. It is that benefit which is being taxed; it is not what the employer has to pay for the car that is involved. What is the value to the employee, that is the question? You may have two salesmen working for competing companies. There may be more advantages to one company in leasing cars than the other because one is bigger and is entitled to a fleet discount.
There are no hard and fast rules which apply to leasing vehicles. We have two salesmen doing the same blessed thing, driving similar cars, yet you are going to charge one more than the other, which is quite conceivable under a leasing agreement, yet the benefit to each is precisely the same. It matters not one whit what the owner or employer has to pay for the vehicle. That has nothing to do with it. What is involved is the benefit to the employee. If a salesman for Procter and Gamble gets a standard Chev. leased by a company, and another salesman gets the same kind of car leased by a much smaller soap distributing company which has to pay more under the leasing agreement, is the minister or the parliamentary secretary saying that the salesman for the smaller company is to be charged more for the benefit he receives? This is patent nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am inclined to agree with the hon. member. This certainly is nonsense. The value of the benefit to the employee is not based on whether he is given precisely the same car as his neighbour. The value to him as an employee is based on a great number of variables, including the amount of use the employee has for the car. Employee "A" may be given exactly the same car model as employee "B", but employee "A" gets considerably more benefit from that car because he drives it 4,000 miles on his annual holiday and things like that, whereas employee "B" does not. So the only criterion from a practical point of view that the income tax department can use in assessing the value of the benefit is the cost to the person providing that benefit. The value to the particular person receiving the benefit depends entirely on how much he uses it. All these are variables which will change from person to person. There is no practical way in which to measure it from that point of view.

Mr. Chairman, once in a while a person has a nightmare in which he dreams he is dealing with tax reform on the floor of the House of Commons. I find myself involved in such a nightmare now. More particularly, my anguish arises out of trying to understand what is meant by subsection (2) at page 55. This is something which has been added to the law and in that sense I suppose it qualifies as reform if one could understand what in effect it means. This deals with the question of what one can claim on the ownership of land. I presume it really is an attempt to control speculation in land, or at least to see that speculation in land does not automatically by itself draw tax benefits, because in part the section provides:
-except to the extent that the taxpayer's gross revenue, if any, from the land for that year exceeds the aggregate of all other amounts deducted in computing his income from the land for that year.
As one goes through the whole thing it is like the music that goes around and around and one wonders where it comes out. I will put my bafflement in this way: Am I correct in understanding it is really to discourage speculation in land, that is, that people simply are not to be allowed to hunt around the edges of our rapidly growing cities, pick up land and enjoy certain tax benefits as a result of so doing? In other words, if land is so acquired it must be land which can bear its share of the taxes of this country? If I have asked the wrong question perhaps the parliamentary secretary could give some enlightenment on th ephilosophy of this subsection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman-
Hear, hear!
The hon. gentleman has returned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, here we are dealing with people who buy land who really are not in the business of dealing with land. That is, they are not in land trading and buying and selling all the time so that they have profits and losses from it but, rather, are buying land on what one might say is a speculative basis. These are people who might write the particular cost against other income. Under the new section this will be added to the inventory value of the land and, when he ultimately sells it, it would be subject to a tax; but this will become part of his costs and not operating expenses which he can write off with other income.

I would not fault the minister for this approach although I believe from a practical sense the once-in-a-lifetime deal in land has attracted income taxes
November 2, 1971

in the past. I am aware of one man in Halifax, for example, who has spent the last 15 years trying to reverse a decision made that long ago. However, I ask: Where does the difference lie between a fellow who jumps in for the purpose of speculation and the fellow who jumps in for the purpose of being a land developer? Does a person have to buy more than one parcel of land in order to qualify in the latter category, or must his income position be different? Or how does he achieve the hallowed position of a respectable land dealer rather than the unhallowed position of a speculator in land?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: The position is exactly the same as under the existing law. Had we moved, as originally proposed in the white paper, to the point where gains were fully taxed, this question would not arise; but in a situation where we are to tax capital gains at half rates we will have the same problem of distinction between what is a capital gain and what is a trading profit as we presently have. Here it is a matter of case law and decisions by the courts.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister indicate if any consideration is being given to the introduction by regulatio nof a more realistic capital cost allowance schedule. Th eproblem to which a solution is addressed arises because an undue and unrealistic amount of capital cost allowance is available for buildings beyond the amount of actual depreciation. It is thi sproblem area which leads to the apparent unfairness in the tax system.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, first of all, it does not apply to this particular section with which we are dealing since it deals with lan donly. I think the whole system of capital cost allowances will have to be reviewed. I should like to emphasize, however, that until this thorough review is carried out there is no intention on the part of the government to change the present capital cost allowance schedules.

Mr. Chairman, I will start right at the very beginning, on section 18 (1) (a). I think this is the area in which one can come up with a personal beef or bleat for Members of Parliament and others who may find themselves in a simila rposition. I would say it is also possible for a member of a provincial legislature to be in a similar position.
The lawyer, the accountant, the medical practitioner or the engineer, by being a full-time parliamentarian, is reduced in his professional capacity to an almost nonoperating basis; he has little or no income from his business or profession. However, he will attend, for instance in the case of lawyers-and remember he does not have an independent office-the annual convention of the Canadian Bar Association because he is particularly interested in this House in being a specialist in, shall we say, the law of the sea, the law of the air or perhaps, now, the law of pollution control. He may be a specialist in criminal law and he will go to the Canadian Bar, but he has little or no professional income: it may be merely
Income Tax Act
nominal and certainly would be less than 50 per cent of his parliamentary stipend.
.50 p.m.)
I put it to the minister that the interpretation of section 18 (l)(a) is that he would not be entitled to his expenses, although there is another section that deals with convention expenses and so forth, yet this is an outlay of expense except to the extent that was made by the taxpayer for the purpose of gaining or producing income from his business or property. He is not gaining any income from his business.
The hon. member for Laurier could attend an annual convention >r some of the periodic conventions of the Canadian Tax Foundation or of the Institute of Chartered Accountants to improve his knowledge so as to make him a better member of the House. I have been to several conferences of the Canadian Tax Foundation and I hope it has given me greater knowledge and greater facility in dealing with tax matters. Yet I have gone to the tax department and they have said I was not entitled because I am not a practising lawyer, my connection with the law firm is purely tenuous because I am a full-time member of the House. I find it rather strange that a Member of Parliament cannot go to one of these professional conferences within his own competence in order to keep himself up to date and to improve his professional knowledge so as to make him a better Member of Parliament. I would like to hear the views of the minister in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would say that hon. members cannot have it both ways. We have an expense allowance which, by legislation, is tax free. If a Member of Parliament is practising law as well as being a Member of Parliament, which many members used to be able to do-I agree that now it is difficult to do so because this is a full time job-he could deduct such expenses as my hon. friend mentioned. If a person has chosen, instead, to be a Member of Parliament he cannot deduct any expenses, but he does have the advantage of the tax free expense allowance.

But that is in connection with many other claims from his constituency. There is no reason why a Member of Parliament should not be on the same basis with regard to attending those conferences as are members of the minister's department who attend these conferences by the dozen.

CRIMINAL CODE-INQUIRY AS TO DEBATE ON ABORTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in deliberately keeping the matter of abortion from being discussed in the House of Commons, the government is guilty of a series of very unfair and very cruel acts. It is forcing unknown numbers of women to bear unwanted children, with all the terrible consequences to them and to society. It is forcing women on low income to face the horrors of a back street operator or the do-it-

yourself procedures which cripple and kill. It is forcing women who can afford it to go to foreign countries for an abortion.
Last year 1,649 Canadian women had to seek such help in New York state. I understand that 44 per cent of them were from the province of Quebec alone. It is forcing uncounted other women to run from hospital to hospital in Canada trying desperately to find one that will help them while the clock ticks remorselessly on and the authorities, with eyes averted from their misery, pass by on the other side.
It is permitting those who are opposed to abortion to force their will on the majority in Canada who believe, equally strongly, that abortion should be legalized. All these things are going on while the government washes its hands and refuses to accept responsibility for a situation which it alone can change. Yet last Friday the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told a high school class in Nova Scotia that women should be the ones to decide whether they should have the legal right to have an abortion if they want one. The young folk applauded loudly, quite unaware of the fact that the Prime Minister is unwilling even to have a debate on abortion in this House this session, as he promised a year ago.
He told the students that he would be very much influenced by the overwhelming feeling of women. He said, "I don't feel I can speak with great authority on this because I am not a woman." Yet when I asked him this afternoon if he would bring in a measure to take abortion from the Criminal Code and allow the elected representatives of the people to vote on it, he completely sidestepped the question. He and his government are the only ones who can bring such a measure before Parliament. Why don't they do it?
To leave the law as it is now simply means that they are on the side of those who are opposed to abortion and are determined to force that position on everyone else, regardless of what it does to women in every part of Canada. Let there be no mistake about that. I can only hope that this attitude will arouse freedom-loving women and men to bring organized pressure on the government in order to show it how wrong it is.
The forces which today are preventing changes in the abortion law are the same ones who for years were successful in keeping birth control illegal and which will resist government action for effective methods of birth control across Canada. These are the forces responsible for unnecessarily large numbers of abortions. These are the forces causing untold suffering and injustice to thousands of women who should have the right to consult their doctors and seek an abortion safely, legally and openly.
On November 20 a large group of Canadian women are coming to Ottawa to impress upon the government the fact, as the Prime Minister told the students in Nova Scotia, that women should be the ones to decide whether they should have the legal right to an abortion. I trust that he will give them that opportunity by having a debate on the subject in Parliament and then by introducing legislation to take abortion out of the Criminal Code and leaving it, as we leave all other medical procedures, a matter between the patient and her doctor, thus allowing both
November 2, 1971

sides to practice their principles freely without either side trying to force its beliefs on the other.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate with the hon. member. This is a subject which raises deep emotions among all of us. I would question the phraseology of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) in saying the government is deliberately postponing facing this issue. The government liberalized the existing legislation and made it far more humane through amendments to the Criminal Code.
In the Speech from the Throne the government said it would set aside a day for debate on this issue, but the fact is that the government simply has not committed itself to further amendments. It said it would set aside a day in the hope that this subject, which is sensitive to all of us, could be aired. Regrettably, the progress of business of the House and the priorities involved have delayed the doing of many things which the government would wish to do. But to say it refuses to accept responsibility is, I think, somewhat unfair. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did, indeed, in Halifax make a statement similar to that attributed to him by the hon. member. But the people in their wisdom have not elected very many women to the House of Commons.

AIR TRANSPORT-NATIONAL POLICY-POSSIBILITY OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIRLINES BECOMING SECOND TRANS-CANADA CARRIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) has escaped back, alive and well, to the mainland from Newfoundland in the company of Mr. Smallwood and that I am to have the pleasure of hearing the parliamentary secretary reply to my question.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The question that I raise at least once a year is about the possible extension of Canadian Pacific Airlines service into Atlantic Canada so that there will be two national airlines serving from coast to coast. The Minister of Transport looked a little askance when I asked this question the other day. He thought that I simply meant to give CPA the profitable run between Montreal and Halifax. I assured him, and this is my view on the subject, that such national service means service from Bonavista to Vancouver Island and from the forty-ninth parallel to as near the North Pole as one can go. Let there be no doubt about that-I am not asking for any privilege for Canadian Pacific Airlines.
If government policy is rearranged in this direction and Canadian Pacific Airlines is allowed to compete in Canada east of Montreal, I hope that it will not compete on the profitable runs only but that it will bear some of the burdens borne by other airlines; in other words, that it will become part of the national air policy to service all parts of Canada. Or, to put it in more vulgar terms, I hope that it has to take the skim milk as well as the cream.
I raise this matter because I think the feelings of opposition members should be made known on national matters and should be placed on the record. I know that aviation economics is not the most delightful subject for a company controller to dabble in, that airlines are having a great deal of trouble making profits, that the regional airlines play a most important part in the Canadian picture, and that in Atlantic Canada Eastern Provincial Airways has done a tremendous job. One cannot simply ask Canadian Pacific to burst holus-bolus into the picture; the economics of airline transportation must be considered carefully before any such decision is made.
It should also be noted clearly for the record that there must be a cabinet directive before the Canadian Transport Commission can even consider extending Canadian Pacific Airlines service in eastern Canada. If the cabinet is silent on the matter, Mr. Pickersgill, as head of the Canadian Transport Commission, will be justified in refusing to consider the matter at all. I know the Minister of Transport was not quite as frank as he usually is when dealing with the question asked in this regard the other day by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). He seemed to imply that the cabinet does not have a role in this, whereas I suggest that it does.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks this evening arise out of a question I put to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) last Friday. It related to the imminent lay-off of 665 workers at the General Motors Plant at Ste. Therese, Quebec. I asked the minister if he would consider the argument put forward to him personally by representatives of local 1163 of the United Auto Workers. The argument was to the effect that if all workers worked a shorter work week, no lay-offs would be necessary. The minister replied that this would not be practical, for if this were done for one industry it would have to be done for all such industries facing lay-offs. The answer also implied that it would be too costly.
I would like to outline the argument put forward by local 1163 to the minister. The proposal by the union local was based on research carried out by Professor Sydney Inkerman of McGill University. Now that the 665 workers have been laid off they will be receiving $77 per man per week in unemployment insurance benefits. Based on a six-month period, which is a reasonable assumption, this expenditure will cost the federal government $1,331,330. Some of this money will go back to both the federal and Quebec governments to the extent of $83,802 in taxes.
For their computations, the union uses as its example one married man with a child. In the brief the union stated that the family would be paying $100 per month for rent and $151 for food, for a total of $251 per month. The remaining income from unemployment insurance would be taxed for such things as clothes, cigarettes, gas, etc. The union argued that the company should not lay off anybody but that all should work a four-day week. In addition, the government would pay 80 per cent of the net earnings for all employees for the fifth day.
The cost to the government, over the same six-month period, would be $1,311,336. This alone would be a saving to the government of $20,000. In addition, the 665 workers, over the six-month period, would contribute $28,528 to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This, coupled with the employer's contributions, would amount to

$57,057. Now that the 665 workers have been laid off, these contributions are lost. Moreover, if the men laid off had been kept on the job they would be paying $28,129 to the Quebec pension fund and, with comparable contributions from the company, the total contribution would be $56,259. Again, this money has been lost due to the lay-off.
The amount of money the laid-off workers would have paid in the form of federal income taxes, had they been employed over these six months, would amount to $295,659. Another sum of $197,970 would have been paid into Quebec income taxes. Again, this money has been lost. In addition, if these 665 men were still employed they would have had $312 left over after food and rent costs each month. Over a six-month period the 665 men now laid off would have had $1,244,999 to pump into the consumer market. Sales taxes would have amounted to $99,599. Medicare contributions, now lost, would amount to another $45,645 from both employer and employees. Had the UAW, local 1163, recommendations been accepted it is very possible that the federal government would have received $352,716 in revenue and the Quebec government would have received an added $399,475, for a grand total of $752,191 in revenue.
So far as the company is concerned, by accepting the union argument or proposal it would have taken 39.2 hours of labour per unit-in this case, per automobile- but under the present situation, with the lay-off of 665 men it is going to take 42 hours of labour per unit.
Mr. Speaker, cost of materials would remain the same, operating overhead or fixed costs would remain the same. In short, and in conclusion, the UAW's proposal would not have cost the company any more, neither would it have cost the government any more. But now that 665 men have been laid off the government will lose income tax revenue, it will have to pay out benefits in unemployment insurance, purchasing power has been reduced, the Quebec pension fund will suffer and Quebec medicare premium income also will suffer.
